MCP.explanation: Model Context Protocol is an open standard connecting AI models to external tools and data
points: Open protocol created by Anthropic to standardize how LLMs connect to tools, data, and actions
Enables AI agents to read files, call APIs, search the web, query databases, and more — all through one consistent interface
Designed to be transport-agnostic (stdio for local, HTTP/SSE for remote)
Already adopted by Claude Desktop, Cursor, Continue.dev, and many open-source projects
Goal is to become the universal USB-C-like connector for AI capabilities

MCP Server.explanation: An MCP server exposes tools, resources, and prompts that any compatible AI client can use
points: Lightweight process or cloud service that implements the MCP spec
Advertises its capabilities (tools, resources, prompts) during handshake
Can run locally (stdio) or remotely (HTTP + SSE)
Examples: filesystem server, Git server, Slack server, database bridge
Security boundary — each server controls exactly what it exposes

MCP Client.explanation: MCP clients like Claude Desktop connect to servers to access their capabilities and data
points: Any LLM frontend that speaks the MCP protocol (Claude Desktop, VS Code extensions, custom agents)
Discovers available servers and their tools/resources/prompts automatically
Handles tool calls, resource reads, progress updates, and cancellations
Manages multiple simultaneous server connections
Responsible for user consent and permission flows

Tools.explanation: MCP Tools let AI models execute functions like file operations, API calls, and web searches
points: Functions the model can call — defined with JSON Schema for name, description, parameters
Can be read-only (get data) or write-capable (create, update, delete)
Executed by the server — model never runs code directly
Support parallel calls, streaming results, progress reporting, and cancellation
Annotated with annotations (read-only, destructive, high-latency, etc.)

Resources.explanation: MCP Resources expose data sources like files, databases, and APIs to AI models
points: Read-only data endpoints — files, database views, API responses, live feeds
Accessed via URI (static or templated with parameters)
Can be injected automatically into context or fetched on demand
Support pagination, binary content (base64), and subscriptions for live updates
Examples: local filesystem, Google Drive folder, Notion database, Git repo

Prompts.explanation: MCP Prompts are reusable prompt templates that standardize AI model behavior across apps
points: Server-provided prompt templates with named arguments
Users select them from a menu in the client UI
Arguments get interpolated → consistent behavior across clients
Great for domain-specific agents (code review, legal doc analysis, medical note summarization)
Can include instructions, few-shot examples, tool-use guidelines

Sampling.explanation: MCP Sampling lets servers request LLM completions through the connected client
points: Server → client request: “please generate text with these instructions”
Enables server-side chaining, reflection, critique, or planning
Client decides model, temperature, max tokens, etc.
Used for agentic loops, self-critique, multi-agent systems
Keeps heavy reasoning on the powerful client side

Transport.explanation: MCP supports stdio and HTTP with SSE transports for client-server communication
points: stdio → local servers (fast, secure, no network)
HTTP + SSE → remote/cloud servers (streaming, discoverable)
Both use JSON-RPC 2.0 message format
Capability negotiation happens at connection start
Future transports possible (WebSocket, gRPC, etc.)

Claude Desktop.explanation: Claude Desktop natively supports MCP letting you connect local and remote MCP servers
points: First major client with built-in MCP support (Anthropic)
Connects to local stdio servers and remote HTTP/SSE servers
Shows server list, tools, resources, prompts in UI
Handles permissions, progress, cancellations, logs
Primary way most users experience MCP today

MCP SDK.explanation: The official MCP SDK lets developers build servers and clients in Python and TypeScript
points: Official libraries: Python (mcp), TypeScript (@anthropic-ai/mcp)
Handles protocol details: handshake, JSON-RPC, SSE, errors
Provides high-level abstractions: @tool, @resource, @prompt decorators
Includes reference servers (filesystem, memory, sequential-thinking)
Open source on GitHub under Anthropic organization

Tool Call.explanation: A tool call is when an AI model invokes an MCP tool and waits for the result
points: Model decides to call a tool based on user request and available tools
Client sends structured JSON-RPC request to the correct server
Server executes the function and returns result (or error)
Model receives result and continues reasoning or responds to user
Supports parallel calls — multiple tools at once

Tool Result.explanation: A tool result is the data returned by an MCP server after executing a tool call
points: Structured JSON response containing success data or error details
Can include text, numbers, arrays, objects, base64 binary
Server can stream partial results for long operations
Model incorporates result into context for next reasoning step
Errors include standard codes (e.g., invalid_input, timeout, permission_denied)

Tool Schema.explanation: Tool schemas define tool names, descriptions, and input parameters using JSON Schema
points: JSON Schema draft 2020-12 used for parameters (type, properties, required, etc.)
Description field is critical — model uses it to decide when to call
Annotations add metadata: read-only, destructive, high-latency, cost
Supports complex types: objects, arrays, enums, oneOf, anyOf
Servers can update schemas dynamically without restarting

SSE Transport.explanation: Server-Sent Events transport lets remote MCP servers stream updates to clients over HTTP
points: HTTP long-polling alternative — unidirectional server → client streaming
Used for progress notifications, partial tool results, live resource updates
Single persistent connection — efficient for real-time feedback
Standard event types: message, error, progress, cancellation
Fallback for clients that don’t support WebSocket

Stdio Transport.explanation: Stdio transport runs MCP servers as local processes communicating through standard input and output
points: Fastest and most secure transport — no network involved
Client spawns server process and pipes stdin/stdout
Ideal for filesystem access, local Git, local DBs
Servers exit when client disconnects (or can persist)
Zero-latency communication compared to HTTP

MCP Host.explanation: An MCP host is the application like Claude Desktop that manages client connections to servers
points: Central coordinator — launches, connects, monitors servers
Handles user-facing UI: server list, permissions, tool selection
Manages multiple connections (local + remote)
Forwards tool calls and receives results
Implements security: user consent, trust levels, revocation

Tool Discovery.explanation: Tool discovery lets AI clients automatically list all tools available on a connected MCP server
points: Client calls list_tools method during/after handshake
Server returns array of tool definitions (name, description, schema, annotations)
Dynamic — tools can appear/disappear without reconnecting
Model uses descriptions to decide which tools are relevant
Foundation for zero-configuration agentic behavior

Resource URI.explanation: Each MCP resource has a unique URI that clients use to read its current content
points: URI format: mcp://server-id/path/to/resource
Static URIs for fixed files/databases, templated URIs for dynamic data
Client calls read_resource(uri) to fetch content
Supports caching hints and ETag-like versioning
Binary resources returned as base64

Resource Templates.explanation: Resource templates are URI patterns that expose dynamic parameterized data sources
points: URI pattern like mcp://server/git/{repo}/commit/{hash}
Parameters passed in path or query string
Server renders dynamic content based on parameters
Great for Git commits, DB queries, API endpoints
Client discovers templates during handshake

Capability Negotiation.explanation: MCP clients and servers negotiate supported capabilities during the initialization handshake
points: Both sides send capability objects on connect
Includes supported transports, versions, features (sampling, subscriptions)
Ensures compatibility before any real work
Future-proof — new capabilities added without breaking old clients
Server can reject connection if required capabilities missing

JSON-RPC.explanation: MCP uses JSON-RPC 2.0 as its message format for all client-server communication
points: Standard JSON-RPC 2.0 — requests, responses, notifications, batches
Method names prefixed (e.g., mcp.list_tools, mcp.read_resource)
Errors follow JSON-RPC standard codes + MCP-specific codes
Supports streaming via SSE for long responses
Lightweight and widely supported

Tool Annotation.explanation: MCP tool annotations describe whether tools are read-only or can modify external state
points: Metadata flags: read_only, destructive, high_latency, high_cost
Helps client decide auto-run vs user confirmation
Can include estimated latency and cost in tokens
Used for trust model and safety layers
Annotations visible to model and user

MCP Inspector.explanation: The MCP Inspector is a developer tool to test and debug MCP servers interactively
points: Web-based GUI for testing MCP servers
Connects to local or remote servers
Lets you call tools, read resources, send prompts manually
Shows raw JSON-RPC messages, errors, logs
Essential for server developers — like Postman for MCP

Roots.explanation: Roots tell MCP servers which directories or resources the client wants them to focus on
points: Client declares “root” URIs at connection (e.g., project folder, Git repo)
Server restricts all paths to subtree of declared roots
Prevents accidental access outside intended scope
Multiple roots allowed (e.g., /home/user/project + /home/user/notes)
Security and context-limiting feature

Server-side Prompts.explanation: Server-side prompts let MCP servers expose templated prompts users can invoke in their AI client
points: Server defines reusable prompt templates with arguments
Client shows them in UI (dropdown or command palette)
User selects prompt + fills arguments → model gets full prompt
Great for consistent workflows (code review, doc generation)
Server can include tool-use instructions in prompt

Elicitation.explanation: MCP elicitation lets servers ask the user for additional information mid-task through the client
points: Server sends elicit message during tool execution
Client shows user prompt (text input, file picker, etc.)
User response sent back to server as tool result
Enables interactive tools (e.g., “which branch?”, “enter API key”)
Keeps human in loop for ambiguous or sensitive steps

Progress Notification.explanation: Progress notifications let MCP servers report long-running task progress back to clients
points: Server sends periodic progress messages (percentage, status, message)
Client displays progress bar or spinner with text
Used for file uploads, long queries, indexing, training
Supports cancellation token — user can stop operation
Improves UX for tools that take >2–3 seconds

Cancellation.explanation: MCP supports cancellation tokens so clients can interrupt long-running server operations
points: Client passes cancellation token with tool call
Server checks token periodically during execution
User clicks “cancel” → client signals cancellation
Server should stop work and return cancelled error
Prevents runaway operations and improves UX

Logging.explanation: MCP servers can send structured log messages to clients for debugging and observability
points: Server sends log messages (info, debug, warning, error)
Client can show in console, save to file, or forward to telemetry
Structured JSON logs — includes timestamp, level, message
Great for diagnosing tool failures or slow performance
Optional — servers can disable when not needed

Pagination.explanation: MCP pagination returns large resource or tool lists in manageable batches via cursor tokens
points: list_tools, list_resources, read_resource support pagination
Server returns cursor token for next page
Client requests next batch with cursor
Prevents memory overload on large directories/repos
Cursor opaque — server controls pagination logic

Authentication MCP.explanation: MCP servers can require OAuth 2.1 authentication before granting AI clients access
points: Server can request OAuth flow during handshake
Client opens browser for user login → gets token
Token sent in Authorization header for subsequent calls
Supports refresh tokens and scopes
Standard way to secure remote/cloud MCP servers

Remote MCP Server.explanation: Remote MCP servers run in the cloud and connect over HTTP giving AI access to remote services
points: Hosted on Vercel, Cloudflare, Fly.io, etc.
Use HTTP + SSE transport
Require authentication (OAuth usually)
Expose cloud services: GitHub, Notion, Slack, Google Drive
Discoverable via registries (Smithery, etc.)

Local MCP Server.explanation: Local MCP servers run on your machine with stdio transport and access local files and apps
points: Run as subprocess via stdio transport
Full access to local filesystem, Git, databases, apps
No network latency — very fast
No authentication needed (localhost)
Examples: filesystem, Git, local DB, local browser

MCP Registry.explanation: MCP registries are directories of published servers that users can discover and install easily
points: Central place to find community and official MCP servers
Includes metadata: name, description, author, capabilities
One-click install in Claude Desktop and other clients
Examples: Smithery, Anthropic registry, community repos
Helps ecosystem growth — like npm for MCP

Smithery.explanation: Smithery is a popular marketplace for discovering and deploying MCP servers
points: First major MCP server registry/marketplace
Browse, search, one-click install servers
Includes both community and verified servers
Shows popularity, last updated, capabilities
Handles remote server deployment (Vercel integration)

MCP over REST.explanation: MCP can be layered over REST APIs to expose existing HTTP services as AI-callable tools
points: Wrap existing REST API as MCP server
Auto-generate tool schemas from OpenAPI spec
Model calls tools → server translates to HTTP request
Enables instant AI access to any REST service
Tools like openapi-to-mcp automate conversion

Tool Composition.explanation: Tool composition chains multiple MCP tool calls together to complete complex multi-step tasks
points: Model calls tool A → uses result to call tool B → etc.
Enables multi-step reasoning and workflows
Server can also compose tools internally
Examples: search → read page → summarize → save
Foundation for agentic behavior

Context Injection.explanation: MCP resources inject relevant live data into the AI's context automatically before it responds
points: Host auto-injects resource content before model sees prompt
Keeps context fresh — no stale data
Used for project files, recent Git changes, Notion notes
Reduces manual copy-paste by user
Configurable per conversation or globally

File System Server.explanation: The official MCP filesystem server exposes local files and directories as readable resources
points: Official reference server — ships with Claude Desktop
Exposes local folders as MCP resources
Model can read any file in allowed roots
Supports binary files (images base64)
Security via root declarations

Git MCP Server.explanation: Git MCP servers expose repository history, branches, and diffs as tools for AI code assistants
points: Local Git repo access via MCP
Tools: get_commit, get_diff, list_branches, checkout
Resources: file contents at any commit
Enables AI code review, debugging, refactoring
Common in Cursor, Continue.dev, Claude Desktop

GitHub MCP Server.explanation: The GitHub MCP server lets AI create issues, pull requests, and manage code repositories
points: Remote GitHub access via OAuth
Tools: create_issue, create_pr, comment, search_repos
Resources: repo files, issues, PRs
Popular for AI-powered GitHub workflows
Official + community versions available

Database MCP Server.explanation: Database MCP servers let AI query PostgreSQL, MySQL, or SQLite to answer data questions
points: Exposes SQL query tool + schema resource
Supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, DuckDB
Model writes SQL → server executes safely
Great for business intelligence, data analysis
Row limits and read-only mode for safety

Browser MCP Server.explanation: Browser MCP servers give AI tools to navigate web pages, click elements, and extract content
points: Headless browser control via MCP
Tools: navigate, click, type, screenshot, extract_text
Enables web research, form filling, scraping
Used in agentic web automation
Security: runs in sandbox or user browser
